cues.text: For over a thousand years, the popes had ruled the Papal States , a substantial swath of central Italy stretching from Rome to Bologna, as sovereign temporal princes.

The nineteenth-century movement for Italian unification (the Risorgimento), led by figures such as Camillo Cavour and Giuseppe Garibaldi under King Victor Emmanuel II of Piedmont-Sardinia, viewed papal temporal rule as the chief obstacle to a unified Italian nation.
By 1860, Piedmontese forces had annexed most of the Papal States' outlying provinces, defeating papal troops at Castelfidardo.
They reduced Pope Pius IX 's temporal domain to Rome and its immediate surroundings, protected for a time only by a French garrison stationed there at Napoleon III's order.
When the Franco-Prussian War forced Napoleon III to withdraw his troops from Rome in 1870, Victor Emmanuel's government seized the opportunity.

On September 20, 1870 , Italian artillery breached the ancient walls near the Porta Pia, and Italian troops occupied the city after only token resistance from the small papal garrison, formally ending more than a millennium of papal temporal sovereignty.

Pius IX refused to recognize the seizure or to accept the Italian government's unilateral Law of Guarantees, which offered him certain privileges and an annual indemnity in exchange for accepting the loss of Rome.
Instead, he confined himself to the Vatican for the rest of his pontificate, declaring himself a 'prisoner of the Vatican' .
His successors Leo XIII, Pius X, Benedict XV, and Pius XI would maintain this self-imposed status for nearly sixty years.
The resulting impasse, known as the Roman Question , poisoned relations between the Holy See and the Italian state for decades.

Popes forbade Catholic participation in Italian national politics (the non expedit ), while the Vatican pressed unsuccessfully for international recognition of its independence and territorial claims.

The Roman Question remained unresolved until the Lateran Treaty of 1929, when Pope Pius XI and Mussolini's government finally settled the dispute, creating the sovereign Vatican City State in exchange for the papacy's formal recognition of the Kingdom of Italy.

The nearly six-decade standoff shaped the modern papacy's self-understanding as a spiritual rather than a great territorial power, a shift historians have called the definitive end of the medieval union of papal spiritual and temporal rule.
